newsitem.title: USA: U.S. negotiators say main talks to start this week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. negotiators say main talks to start this week.

text.p: Congressional tax negotiators who met throughout the weekend with White House officials said Sunday the prep work is done and they will get down to the nitty gritty this week on tax cut legislation.

"We've at least got to the point to where they (administration) are in the position where they say they will be able to negotiate," House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer said after the Sunday evening meeting.
"This is the first time tonight that we've been able to get into that posture," the Texas Republican added.

Substantive negotiations were expected to get under way early this week toward crafting a final five-year $85 billion net tax cut bill as called for by the May budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House.

"Basically what we're trying to do is sit down and talk and ferret out where the differences are," said Sen. William Roth, a Delaware Republican, who chairs the House-Senate conference on the tax bill.
"We haven't been negotiating in the strict sense of the word," he added, referring to the weekend meetings.

Roth put a discussion draft on the table Friday that condensed by $10 billion over 10 years his priority proposals for expanding Individual Retirement Accounts. The draft was described as just a step to get talks started rather than a negotiating stance.

The three-pronged nature of the tax cut talks have added a new element this year because not only are the House and Senate trying to work out differences in their two bills, but the White House is also involved at this stage.

The Roth draft moved toward the administration on the IRAs, but away and toward the House on the $500 per-child tax credit by proposing low-income working families take 75 percent of their earned income tax credit and then be eligible for the child tax credit if they owe income tax.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and other administration officials brought a letter from President Clinton Saturday that stated his guiding principles for tax legislation.

"The administration now is moving away from the discussion stage and talking about negotiating and that is very, very constructive," Archer said. "So far they have simply restated what their positions are and they have not advanced anything new," he added.
"I think we moved forward," John Hilley, White House legislative director, said Sunday evening.
Representative Charles Rangel of New York, the senior Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, said: "I'm not overly impressed with the progress that's been made this evening."

House and Senate tax conferees will try to work out lower-tier issues Monday. Republicans have said they want the tax legislation completed by the end of this week so it can go before the full Congress before the August recess.
"We only have two weeks and we have to get things finished by the end of the week," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican said.

The Roth discussion draft would also change provisions in the proposed tax legislation to focus corporate alternative minimum tax relief on small businesses, eliminate capital gains tax relief for venture capital, and drop "indexing" to take into account effects of inflation for the corporate capital gains tax.

The Roth draft also proposed the threshold at which the estate tax kicks in for family farms and businesses be phased up to $900,000 from the current $600,000 instead of immediately increasing to $1 million as in the Senate bill.
